Nothing to count yet: matches against the Bot count once they reach the target, Klondike games count when you win them or give them up.

Games won are in yellow. In matches against the Bot only those that reach the target are counted: the ones left half way do not count. In Klondike a game counts as lost only if you give it up by dealing a new one.
Reset all statistics? This cannot be undone.

Two players, 40-card deck. Four cards face up on the table, three each in hand.
Players take turns playing one card. If a table card has the same value, you capture it. If not, you can capture several cards whose values add up to the card you played: the Ace is 1, the Knave 8, the Knight 9, the King 10. If a single card of the same value is there, that one takes precedence and must be captured. If you capture nothing, your card stays on the table.
Clearing the table with a capture is a SWEEP, worth one point. It does not count on the last card of the game.

When the three cards in hand run out, three more are dealt to each player, as long as the deck lasts: each round of three cards is a hand. When the deck is empty and the last three have been played, the game ends: whatever is left on the table goes to whoever captured last.

At the end of the game four points are counted, one each: most cards, most coins, the settebello (the 7 of coins), and the primiera. Plus the sweeps. On a tie, nobody takes that point.
The primiera is worked out by taking your best card in each suit and adding up their values: the 7 is worth 21, the 6 is 18, the Ace 16, the 5 is 15, the 4 is 14, the 3 is 13, the 2 is 12, the figures 10. A player who captured no card at all in one suit does not compete for the primiera.

The match goes to whoever reaches 11 or 21 points first, whichever you choose in the settings.

Two players, 40-card deck. Three cards each, the rest forms the deck. The bottom card of the deck is left face up: its suit is the briscola, the trump, and it beats every other suit.
One player leads a card, the other answers with whatever they like: you are not obliged to follow suit. The trick goes to the higher trump, or, if there is none, to the higher card of the led suit. Whoever takes the trick draws first and leads the next one. Once the deck runs out, the last hand is played: three cards each, no drawing.

Order of strength, highest first: Ace, 3, King, Knight, Knave, 7, 6, 5, 4, 2.

Points: Ace 11, the 3 is worth 10, King 4, Knight 3, Knave 2. The other cards are worth nothing. There are 120 points in all: 61 are enough to win the game, and at 60 all the game is a draw.

The match goes to whoever wins 5 or 11 games first, whichever you choose in the settings.

Two players, 40-card deck. Ten cards each, twenty stay in the stock.

Whoever answers MUST follow the led suit. You may play another suit only if you have none of it, but then you cannot take the trick.

The trick goes to the higher card of the led suit. Then both draw, the winner first, and the drawn card is shown to the opponent: keep an eye on them, they tell you what is left in their hand. Once the stock runs out, the last hand is played: ten tricks with no drawing.

Order of strength, highest first: 3, 2, Ace, King, Knight, Knave, 7, 6, 5, 4.

Points: the Ace is worth a whole point; the 2, the 3, the Knave, the Knight and the King are worth a third each; from 4 to 7, nothing. The last trick is worth one point. At the end of the game each player drops the leftover thirds, and the game is always worth 11 points in all.

The match goes to whoever reaches 21 or 31 points first, whichever you choose in the settings.

GLOSSARY

Hand: the cards you hold: three in Scopa and Briscola, ten in Tresette, five in 5-Card Draw, two in Texas Hold'em. In poker a single deal, betting rounds included, is also called a hand.
Game: the whole deck, from the deal to counting the points. In poker it is instead the series of deals, and it ends when only one player is left with chips.
Match: the series of games up to the target. Poker has none, because the game is already a series. The statistics count finished matches and, for poker, finished games.

IN POKER, ALSO

Chip: the token you bet with. Pot: what you win. Ante: what everyone puts in before seeing the cards, in 5-Card Draw. Blinds: the two forced bets that do the same job in Texas. All-in: betting everything you have. Side pot: the part of the pot a player who went all-in cannot win, because from each opponent you win at most as much as you put in yourself.

RESPECT FOR YOUR PRIVACY

This app collects nothing and sends nothing. There are no usage statistics, no advertising, no third-party tracking, and it asks for no permissions. It has no access to the internet, nor to your contacts, your location, the camera or the files on your phone. You can check this yourself in the Android settings, under the app's Permissions.
The only thing the app saves is your game preferences, and they stay on your phone.

RESPONSIBLE PLAY

In poker, in this app, you do bet: the word is worth saying rather than dancing around it. But you bet with chips that are not money. They cannot be bought, they cannot be topped up by paying, they convert into nothing and they never leave this phone. When they run out the game is lost, and the next one starts again from scratch, free. There is no way to spend real money in this app, and there will not be one: there are no purchases, no advertising, and with no internet access there could not be either.

That said, poker is the card game that comes closest to gambling, and the reasoning that helps you learn here - working out the odds, deciding how much to risk - is the same reasoning that makes gambling attractive elsewhere. If playing here leaves you thinking about playing for money somewhere else, that is the moment to stop and to talk to someone about it.

The reminder between one game and the next is still there, and it can be turned off in the settings. In poker it appears when the game closes, that is when only one player is left with chips.
The Bot\'s cards stay face up and fully visible. Useful for checking the game logic.
The program plays both the Bot\'s cards and yours. Useful for testing quickly that everything works.
At the end of every match a reminder appears and you have to wait a minute before starting again. If you turn it off, it comes back on by itself after an hour.

Playing for a long time without stopping can turn into a habit that is hard to keep in check. Stop for a minute: stand up, have a drink, look at the time.

If you feel the need to start again straight away, if you are playing to make up for a loss, or if playing is taking time away from other things, talk to someone about it.

Italy's national freephone helpline for gambling-related problems: 800 558 822 (free and anonymous, Monday to Friday, 10am to 4pm). Outside Italy, look for the equivalent service in your own country.

A solitaire played with the 52-card French deck. The aim is to build all four foundations, top right, from Ace to King.

Seven columns: the first with one card, the seventh with seven. Only the last card of each column is face up. The remaining 24 form the stock, top left.

The columns are built downwards in alternating colours: a black 8 goes on a red 9. You can move a single card or a group that is already in order.

An empty column takes a King and nothing else. It is the harshest rule in the game: free space is the most valuable thing you have, and only four cards out of fifty-two can use it.

The foundations are built upwards, one suit each, from Ace to King. A card that has gone up can come back down if you need it as a base: just tap it.

The stock is turned by tapping it. When it runs out, tapping the empty space turns it over again: the cards come back in the same order as before. How many are turned at a time, one or three, is chosen in the settings.

You play by tapping, not by dragging. You tap a card and it goes where it makes sense: the foundation first, then a column. If that is not where you wanted it, there is Undo.

When no face-down cards are left and the stock is finished, Finish appears: from there on there are no choices left to make, only cards to send up.

Not every deal can be won, and it is not your fault: about one in eleven is lost from the start when turning one card at a time, about one in five when turning three.

Played with the 52-card French deck, either two-handed against the Bank or four-handed against three programmed opponents, as you choose in the settings. Five cards each, face down.

Before the deal everyone puts an ante of $10 into the pot. It is there so that there is something to win even when everybody folds at once: without it, folding every time would be free and there would be no game.

First betting round. Anyone who does not want to go on folds, and leaves in the pot whatever they have already put in. Those who stay match the highest bet, or raise.

The draw. Once everyone has matched, each player changes from zero to four cards. Standing pat, that is changing none, announces a hand that is already made: how many cards your opponent changes is there for all to see, and it is the most valuable piece of information in the game. It works the other way round too, so mind what you are announcing.

Second betting round, and then whoever is left shows their cards: the pot goes to the best hand.

Betting is fixed-limit: $20 in the first round, $40 in the second, no more than three raises per round. If you do not have enough chips left you bet what you have and go all-in: from each opponent you win at most as much as you put in yourself, and whatever the others put in beyond that forms a side pot they play for among themselves.

Ranking of hands, strongest first: straight flush, four of a kind, full house, flush, straight, three of a kind, two pair, one pair, high card. The Ace is the highest card, but in A 2 3 4 5 it counts as one: that is a straight, and it is five high.

Bluffing is part of the game, and the Bank bluffs. This is not a concession to realism: an opponent who only bets with good hands can be read in ten hands, and never getting paid for your good hands is the most expensive mistake in poker. With On-screen odds switched on you can see what your hand is worth, whether calling pays, and how often that bet from the Bank is on nothing.

The game ends when only one player is left with chips.

Played with the 52-card French deck, either two-handed against the Bank or four-handed against three programmed opponents, as you choose in the settings. Two cards face down each, and five face up in the middle of the table that count for everyone: your hand is the best five of the seven you can see.

Instead of an ante there are the blinds: two forced bets of $10 and $20, posted before anyone sees a card. Who posts them changes every hand, because the dealer moves round one seat, so the turn comes to everybody.

Four betting rounds, with the community cards turned up in between:

Pre-flop: you have only your own two cards.
Flop: three are turned up at once.
Turn: the fourth.
River: the fifth and last.

In each round anyone who does not want to go on folds. If nobody has bet you may check, putting in nothing, and play moves on. After the river whoever is left shows their cards.

Betting is fixed-limit: $20 in the first two rounds, $40 in the last two, no more than three raises per round. All-in and side pots work as in 5-Card Draw: from each opponent you win at most as much as you put in yourself.

Ranking of hands, strongest first: straight flush, four of a kind, full house, flush, straight, three of a kind, two pair, one pair, high card. The Ace is the highest card, but in A 2 3 4 5 it counts as one: that is a straight, and it is five high.

The five community cards belong to everybody, so ties are common here: if two hands are equal the highest card that tells them apart decides, and if there is none the pot is split.

Bluffing is part of the game, and the Bank bluffs: more here than in Draw, because the community cards let you tell a story about a hand you do not hold. With On-screen odds switched on you can see what your hand is worth and whether calling pays.

The game ends when only one player is left with chips.
Three at a time is much harder: two thirds of the stock never reach the top during the current pass, and the deals that cannot be won go from about one in eleven to about one in five.
Shows what your hand is worth and the odds above which calling pays. It is there to teach: they are the same numbers the Bank reasons with.
